title: Player Battles: Schedule Math That Decides Draft Picks
excerpt: Ten close draft decisions where schedule fit can break a tie between similarly productive players.
author: Cracked Ice Analytics
content:
> Archive note: This article analyzes the 2025–26 schedule. Player teams, roles, and projections may have changed. Use the current [player comparison tool](/compare) for 2026–27 decisions.


Two players can have similar production and radically different fantasy value once their schedules meet your lineup. The useful question is not only “Who scores more per game?” It is also “How many of those games can my roster actually use?”

## The tiebreaker most rankings omit

Cracked Ice separates three ideas:

1. **NHL games:** the number on a team’s schedule.
2. **Off-night games:** games on quieter NHL nights, when fantasy lineups usually have more room.
3. **Usable starts:** games that survive your league’s date window, active slots, position eligibility, and existing roster congestion.

Schedule should not turn a weak player into an early pick. It should break close calls and reveal when a slightly lower per-game scorer can produce more total value in your lineup.

## Apply the method to your league

Compare players using your scoring settings and dates, then test the same decision under a regular-season, playoff, or balanced strategy. Treat availability as league-specific: a player named here may not be available in yours.

title: Zero Bench: A Schedule-First Fantasy Hockey Mock Draft
excerpt: A 2025–26 experiment in drafting for usable games instead of collecting the highest names on a ranking list.
author: Cracked Ice Analytics
content:
> Archive note: This mock draft used the 2025–26 schedule. It remains useful as a strategy example, but its team and player recommendations are not current.


The experiment was simple: build a competitive roster while reducing the number of games stranded on the bench. A fantasy roster does not score for every NHL game its players play. Busy Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays create collisions; quieter nights create room.

## The governing rule

Production remains the foundation. Schedule fit becomes more important as players get closer in projected value and as the roster fills. Early picks should secure elite production. Middle and late picks can deliberately fill schedule and position gaps.

## What a schedule-first draft changes

- It values multi-position eligibility because one player can fill more open slots.
- It treats playoff games and off-nights as a strategy input, not a guarantee.
- It delays a crowded position when a comparable tier will remain available.
- It measures the games your lineup can start instead of assuming every scheduled game counts.

The result is not literally a roster with zero bench decisions. It is a roster engineered to waste fewer opportunities.

title: Best Position Group Stacks for Fantasy Hockey 2025–26
excerpt: How complementary team schedules can create more usable starts within a position group.
author: Cracked Ice Analytics
content:
> Archive note: This article uses the 2025–26 schedule. The position-stack concept still applies, but the examples should not be used as current recommendations.


When two or more players compete for the same fantasy slots, their team schedules determine how many games can reach your active lineup. A third center who often plays on the same nights as your first two centers may spend more time on the bench than a comparable player whose team fills quieter dates.

## What makes a useful position stack

- Strong enough per-game production for the acquisition cost.
- Fewer shared game dates within the position group.
- More games on off-nights.
- Eligibility that can move between active slots.
- A schedule that still works during your fantasy playoffs.

The schedule cannot predict injuries, role changes, or performance. It can quantify opportunity. Use that information as a tiebreaker after accounting for player quality and league scoring.
